stimulus.text:
Dunmore: “And I do hereby further declare all indentured Servants, Negroes, or others, (appertaining to Rebels,) free that are able and willing to bear Arms, they joining His MAJESTY'S Troops as soon as may be, for the more speedily reducing this Colony to a proper Sense of their Duty, to His MAJESTY'S Crown and Dignity.” — Lord Dunmore's Proclamation, November 7, 1775 (abridged)

Virginia Convention: “We think it proper to declare, that all slaves who have been, or shall be seduced, by his lordship's proclamation, or other arts, to desert their masters' service, and take up arms against the inhabitants of this colony, shall be liable to such punishment as shall hereafter be directed by the General Convention. . . . we hereby promise pardon to them, they surrendering themselves to Col. William Woodford, or any other commander of our troops, and not appearing in arms after the publication hereof.” — Virginia Convention, December 14, 1775 (abridged)
stimulus.source_note: Lord Dunmore's Proclamation, November 7, 1775, and Virginia Convention declaration, December 14, 1775. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Lord Dunmore's Proclamation (November 7, 1775) and the Virginia Convention's reply (December 14, 1775), public domain. Different questions from the 3.5 Dunmore set (0510-0512).

stem: The two passages disagree most directly about whether enslaved people who take up arms should be

options.text: Freed for joining the king, or punished for leaving their owners
Allowed to vote in the new Virginia government
options.misconception: Neither passage mentions voting; both are about bearing arms, freedom, and punishment, not the ballot.

options.text: Sent to the West Indies to work on sugar plantations
options.misconception: Neither side proposes sending anyone to the West Indies; the argument is over freedom and punishment in Virginia.

options.text: Given land of their own in the western territory
options.misconception: Neither passage offers land; Dunmore offers freedom for service, and Virginia offers pardon for return.

rationales.A: Dunmore promises freedom to those who join his troops, while Virginia promises punishment to those who desert — and pardon only to those who come back.
rationales.B: Voting appears in neither passage; the fight is over arms, freedom, and punishment.
rationales.C: The West Indies never enter either passage; both sides argue about Virginia, not the sugar islands.
rationales.D: Land is offered by neither side; the choice on the table is freedom for service or pardon for return.
rationales.general:
1. Read Dunmore's offer. Freedom for enslaved people of rebels who bear arms for the king.
2. Read Virginia's answer. Punishment for those who desert, and pardon only for those who return.
3. Name the clash. The same act — taking up arms — earns freedom from one side and punishment from the other.
Remember: when two sources answer the same act in opposite ways, the disagreement is the point.
